previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a complex history of sclerosing mesenteritis, chronic small bowel obstructions, and prior abdominal surgeries was readmitted for recurrent abdominal pain, nausea, and failure to pass flatus, consistent with a functional small bowel obstruction. She was managed conservatively with bowel rest, NG tube decompression, and TPN. After no improvement over the first week, a small bowel follow-through and push enteroscopy showed slow transit without a transition point, confirming a functional obstruction. A G-tube was placed for long-term decompression and hydration via free water flushes. During her stay, she developed transient word-finding difficulties and subjective right-sided weakness; neurologic workup including CT head and CTA head/neck showed no acute findings, with changes attributed to a prior stroke. Her anticoagulation was transitioned from rivaroxaban to therapeutic enoxaparin due to concerns about absorption. Pain was managed with Dilaudid suppositories, and she was discharged home on TPN, G-tube care, and follow-up plans with a new GI surgeon and specialists.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Ms. ___,

It was a pleasure taking care of you here at ___ 
___. You were admitted to our hospital for 
intractable nausea and PO intolerance. You were found to have a 
transient small bowel obstruction with obstruction of your 
gastric tube.  Your gastric tube was upsized. You have recovered 
and are now ready to be discharged to rehab. Please follow the 
recommendations below to ensure a speedy and uneventful 
recovery. 
 

 
ACTIVITY:
 
- Do not drive until you have stopped taking pain medicine and 
feel you could respond in an emergency.
 
- You may climb stairs. 
 
- You may go outside, but avoid traveling long distances until 
you see your surgeon at your next visit.
 
- You may start some light exercise when you feel comfortable.
 
- Heavy exercise may be started after 6 weeks, but use common 
sense and go slowly at first.
 
- You may resume sexual activity unless your doctor has told you 
otherwise.
 

 
HOW YOU MAY FEEL: 
 
- You may feel weak or ""washed out"" for 6 weeks. You might want 
to nap often. Simple tasks may exhaust you.
 
- You may have a sore throat because of a tube that was in your 
throat during hospitalization.
 

 
YOUR BOWELS:
 
- Constipation is a common side effect of medicine such as 
Percocet or codeine. If needed, you may take a stool softener 
(such as Colace, one capsule) or gentle laxative (such as milk 
of magnesia, 1 tbs) twice a day. You can get both of these 
medicines without a prescription.
 
- If you go 48 hours without a bowel movement, or have pain 
moving the bowels, call your surgeon.
 
- After some operations, diarrhea can occur. If you get 
diarrhea, don't take anti-diarrhea medicines. Drink plenty of 
fluitds and see if it goes away. If it does not go away, or is 
severe and you feel ill, please call your surgeon.

- It is critical that you regularly vent our G tube to prevent 
mucus plugging from recurring. 
 

 
PAIN MANAGEMENT:
 
- Your pain should get better day by day. If you find the pain 
is getting worse instead of better, please contact your surgeon.
If you experience any of the folloiwng, please contact your 
surgeon:
 
- sharp pain or any severe pain that lasts several hours
- pain that is getting worse over time
- pain accompanied by fever of more than 101
- a drastic change in nature or quality of your pain
 
MEDICATIONS:
- Take all the medicines you were on before the operation just 
as you did before, unless you have been told differently.
- If you have any questions about what medicine to take or not 
to take, please call your surgeon. 
- You were not given a prescription for dilaudid because you 
indicated that you have several suppositories left at home. 
Please take those as prescribed, not exceeding 3g every 6 hours.

INDICATION:  ___ year old woman with SBO// upsize existing

COMPARISON:  Gastrostomy tube check/replacement/repositioning ___

TECHNIQUE:  OPERATORS: Dr. ___ performed the
procedure. Dr. ___ was available for the trainee during the key components
of the procedure and has reviewed and agrees with the trainee's findings.
ANESTHESIA: Moderate sedation was provided by administrating divided doses of
50 mcg of fentanyl and 0.5 mg of midazolam throughout the total intra-service
time of 20 minutes during which the patient's hemodynamic parameters were
continuously monitored by an independent trained radiology nurse. 1% lidocaine
was injected in the skin and subcutaneous tissues overlying the access site.
MEDICATIONS: None
CONTRAST: 0 ml of Optiray contrast.
FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE:  1.9 min, 5 mGy

PROCEDURE:  1.  Up sizing of pre-existing gastrostomy tube to 16 ___ MIC
gastrostomy tube.

PROCEDURE DETAILS: Following the discussion of the risks, benefits and
alternatives to the procedure, written informed consent was obtained from the
patient. The patient was then brought to the angiography suite and placed
supine on the exam table.  A pre-procedure time-out was performed per ___
protocol. The upper abdomen and tube site was prepped and draped in the usual
sterile fashion.

The existing tube was injected with air and showed appropriate insufflation of
the stomach. The stay sutures were cut. A short Amplatz wire was advanced
through the tube into the stomach. The existing tube was then removed using
gentle traction.  Next, serial dilatation of the tract up to 20 ___ was
then performed.  Then, a 16 ___ MIC gastrostomy tube was advanced
over the wire into the stomach and the balloon was inflated using normal
saline.  Air injection confirmed appropriate position.

Sterile dressing was applied. Patient tolerated the procedure well and there
were no immediate post-procedure complications.

FINDINGS: 

1.  Pre-existing 12 ___ Wills ___ noted to be in appropriate position
(intragastric)
2.  Newly placed 16 ___ MIC gastrostomy tube noted to be in appropriate
positioning after air injection

IMPRESSION: 

Successful upsizing of feeding tube to a 16 ___ MIC gastrostomy tube
